title: II Samuel: A New Translation with Introduction, Notes, and Commentary (The Anchor Bible, vol. 9)
author: P. Kyle McCarter Jr.
allowedUseNotes: Modern copyrighted critical commentary. Project stores only its own summary/paraphrase of McCarter's discussion, with a single short attributed quotation (under 15 words) of his own stated conclusion; no reproduction of his translation, textual notes, or broader commentary.
summary: McCarter's Anchor Bible commentary on 2 Samuel, a standard modern critical reference for the book. On 2 Samuel 1:1-16, McCarter notes the episode's structural resemblance to the messenger scene at 1 Samuel 4:12-17 (the fugitive who brings news of a battlefield disaster) and treats the Amalekite's claim to have killed Saul as fundamentally unresolved by the narrative itself: commenting on whether David was taken in by the messenger's story, McCarter writes that '[w]hether David was deceived or not, we cannot tell' (McCarter, II Samuel, p. 63). This project cites McCarter for that narrower, agnostic point — that a leading modern critical commentary treats the reliability question as genuinely open in the text rather than as a settled harmonization problem — rather than for adopting either of the two more specific scholarlyViews (outright fabrication vs. looter's embellishment of a genuine find) surfaced from the two public-domain commentaries also cited on this claim (Keil & Delitzsch 1866; Gill's Exposition 1748-63). Queue #20a researcher pass (2026-08-12) extended this card's coverage to 2 Samuel 3-4, the chapters covering Abner's break with Ish-bosheth, his death, and Ish-bosheth's assassination. McCarter is the originator of the 'apology of David' reading applied throughout this stretch of text (first argued in his own 1980 Journal of Biblical Literature article, cited on this project as its own card, mccarter-1980-apology-of-david, since it long predates and stands independently of this 1984 commentary) — the thesis that 1-2 Samuel's narration of the convenient deaths of Saul, Abner, and Ish-bosheth is shaped throughout to defend David against real contemporary accusations of having orchestrated them. This project's claim-public-response cites McCarter (via mccarter-1980-apology-of-david) directly for that reading as applied to 2 Samuel 3:36-37's insistence that 'it had not been the king's will to put Abner to death.' A specific, page-verified McCarter comment on the political meaning of Abner's going in to Rizpah (3:6-11, claim-abner-break) or on the 2 Samuel 4:6 MT/LXX textual crux (claim-ish-bosheth-assassination) specifically was searched for but not found via secondary corroboration in this pass, despite McCarter's Anchor Bible commentaries being well documented (via multiple independent secondary sources) as containing systematic verse-by-verse Textual Notes sections that regularly weigh the Old Greek/Qumran witnesses against the Masoretic Text for exactly this kind of crux in Samuel — see this card's confidenceNotes. Queue #22 researcher pass (2026-08-24) extended coverage to 2 Samuel 5, the united-kingdom covenant, the capture of Jerusalem, the Hiram building notice, and the two Rephaim Valley engagements. McCarter's Anchor Bible commentary is a standard critical-commentary venue for the position that tsinnor's precise meaning in 5:8 cannot be recovered with confidence (the third scholarlyView on claim-tsinnor-crux); a specific, page-verified McCarter statement on the word itself was searched for but not found via secondary corroboration this pass (the same 'checked, permanently thin for this specific point' outcome as the 4:6 crux above) — this card is cited on that scholarlyView as representative of the broader critical-commentary position, not as a page-verified direct quotation. McCarter is also cited generally on claim-philistine-reaction and the two Rephaim-engagement claims (the topical-vs-chronological arrangement question at 5:17, and the MT/LXX and Geba/Gibeon textual variants at 5:21 and 5:25) as the standard modern critical-commentary venue for exactly this kind of text-critical and compositional question in Samuel, consistent with how it is already used for 2 Samuel 3-4. A 2026-08-29 researcher pass extended coverage to 2 Samuel 6 and 2 Samuel 7 (only the 7:13a finding below is queue #29 material — the 2 Samuel 6 searches are unrelated, non-queue-numbered gap-closing). For 2 Samuel 6: this pass searched specifically for a named McCarter treatment of three disputed questions already carried unattributed in this project's claims — claim-ark-procession-departure's cart-vs-Numbers-4/7-carrying-poles dispute, and claim-michal-confrontation's literal-vs-rhetorical reading of 6:20b's 'uncovered himself' and its separate 6:23 childlessness-causation question — and did not find a page-verifiable McCarter statement on any of the three via secondary corroboration (see confidenceNotes for the search record). This card's own coverage of 2 Samuel 6 accordingly stays general — McCarter is well documented as continuing his standard verse-by-verse Textual Notes/Comment method through this chapter — rather than pinned to any of those three specific disputes; none of them cite this card as a result. For 2 Samuel 7: this pass did find a specific, cross-corroborated McCarter reading of 7:13a ('he shall build a house for my name'). Multiple independent-looking secondary academic sources describing McCarter's commentary (II Samuel, pp. 217-24 and 222) attribute to him the view that 7:13a functions as an editorial 'linchpin' — a highly redactional half-verse binding together the chapter's two otherwise-incongruous notions (the LORD's refusal of a temple from David personally, vv. 4-7, and the promise of an enduring dynastic 'house' for David instead, vv. 11b-16) — rather than belonging to an earlier, self-contained promise-oracle core. This is a genuine, named-attribution finding for the redaction-critical reading of 7:13a, recorded here for a parallel scene-build session (Milestone 8, nathans-oracle) to cite once claim-nathan-oracle exists; this card does not add that claim itself, out of this pass's scope. McCarter's commentary is also independently documented as attributing the sanctuary/tent-and-tabernacle language elsewhere in the chapter to Priestly material no earlier than the sixth century BCE, while treating the oracle's core dynastic-promise themes as pre-Deuteronomistic in origin — a general compositional-layering treatment of the chapter's covenant theology (the house/house wordplay, the dynastic promise) consistent with, but broader than, the 7:13a point specifically.
confidenceNotes: Bibliographic details (title, publisher, year, Anchor Bible volume number) and the page-63 quotation are drawn from secondary/tertiary web sources quoting and citing McCarter directly (cross-corroborated across independent search results, including a citation of this line in Pamela Tamarkin Reis's 2006 Journal for the Study of the Old Testament article 'Killing the Messenger: David's Policy or Politics?'), not from direct page-by-page inspection of the 1984 Doubleday print volume. The 4:6 MT/LXX crux and the Abner-Rizpah political-claim reading were both searched for specifically and not landed on a page-verifiable McCarter citation in this pass — closed as checked, permanently thin for this card's own coverage of those two specific points (see claim-ish-bosheth-assassination and claim-abner-break, which cite other named sources for those two points instead). TO VERIFY if a primary or fuller-text copy becomes accessible. Queue #22 pass (2026-08-24): the extension to 2 Samuel 5 was corroborated by cross-checking multiple independent secondary web sources describing this commentary's continued verse-by-verse method and its standard status in Samuel scholarship, not by primary-copy inspection. A specific, page-verifiable McCarter statement on tsinnor (5:8) was searched for directly and not found via secondary corroboration — closed as checked, permanently thin for that specific named-attribution question, the same outcome pattern as the 4:6 crux; this card's use on claim-tsinnor-crux is as a representative venue for the 'meaning not recoverable' critical-commentary position generally, not a verified direct quotation. TO VERIFY the same way as the rest of this card if a primary or fuller-text copy becomes accessible. 2026-08-29 researcher pass (not a queue-numbered item): the 2 Samuel 6 search (cart-vs-carrying-poles, 'uncovered himself,' and the 6:23 causation question) was genuinely attempted across roughly a dozen differently-worded web searches and did not surface a page-verifiable McCarter statement on any of the three — closed as checked, permanently thin for named-attribution purposes on this card, the same outcome pattern as the 4:6 crux. Unlike the tsinnor crux, though, this card is deliberately not added to claim-ark-procession-departure's or claim-michal-confrontation's sourceIds at all: no evidence surfaced that McCarter addresses any of the three points even at the general-representative-venue level this card's tsinnor-crux citation relies on, so even that weaker citation would overstate what this pass actually found. The 2 Samuel 7:13a finding is corroborated across two independent-looking secondary academic sources (a Trinity Western University master's-level thesis on the dynastic oracle in Samuel-Kings, and a Penn State University dissertation's treatment of the same chapter) that both describe McCarter's 'linchpin' reading of 7:13a and both point to the same page range (McCarter, II Samuel, pp. 217-24, 222) — not from direct inspection of the 1984 volume itself, and not fully independent of each other (both may draw on the same underlying scholarly-reception description of McCarter's argument rather than each having checked his text separately). TO VERIFY: exact page-by-page wording of the 'linchpin' argument against a primary or fuller-text copy, and whether the two secondary sources are independently sourced or one is citing the other.
